utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-11-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good evening, Your Honours. On behalf of the Prosecution my name is Alex Whiting. I'm joined this evening by Ms. Nisha Valabhji on my right, Mr. Colin Black, and our case manager, Ms. Lakshmie Walpita.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Your Honours. I am attorney-at-law Predrag Milovancevic, counsel for Mr. Milan Martic. I hail from Belgrade. I'm joined by my co-counsel, attorney-at-law Vuk Sekulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the situation about the accused. Is that Mr. Martic at the back?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I could put a few questions to Mr. Martic before we start. Mr. Martic, how are you in health?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't like to talk about this matter, but I am fine, I suppose you could say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have no complaints about your detention circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no objections. As for the rest, you could say that everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. Can I just make sure that we all have the same copy of the agenda. Mr. Whiting, do you have a copy of the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. It was e-mailed to us. It's dated today 12 December 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's correct. And you too, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, we do have an agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Thank you, sir. Okay. Now, can I confirm also that we are all using the Second Amended Indictment, supposedly dated the 14th of July, 2003, which was filed by the Registry on the 9th of December to correct an error in the pagination. Is that correct? Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is the -- that's the operative indictment, and, to be clear, it's my understanding, as I'm sure it is the Court's understanding, that the version that was filed just a few days ago is identical to the version that has been in existence since the 14th of July, 2003, just -- there was -- as the Court indicated, an issue about the pagination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And you confirm that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have the Second Amended Indictment in front of us, the one that was now referred to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Under item 4, proceedings in Croatia against the accused concerning Zagreb bombing, I just -- the Tribunal has been advised at the provisional hearing on the 23rd of September 2003 this issue of the indictment against the accused and his conviction in absentia was discussed. Now, as far as the Trial Chamber has been able to assert -- know or pursuant to Rule 13 has been issued, could the Prosecution and the Defence clarify this matter for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The -- the conviction in absentia that the Court is referring, I believe, at least the one that was discussed in context of provisional release does not relate to the Zagreb bombing in 1995. It relates to events that occurred in Croatia in 1990 and 1991. The actual judgement of the court was attached to the accused's motion for leave to appeal the provisional release decision of the Trial Chamber. So it is -- the decision of the Court in Croatia is actually in the record. I have it in front of me and I don't believe -- it pertains basically to the role of the accused and others in creating a separate state within Croatia and splitting away in violation of the constitution and the laws of Croatia. It does not pose any problem from our perspective, in our view, with respect to proceeding on this indictment under the Statute. There is no -- it did not address the crimes that are charged in the indictment that is here before this court and that therefore we would see no prohibition on proceeding with the indictment that's before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you have any comment to make on that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I confirm what my learned friend from the OTP has just said. That indictment contains no reference to the shelling of Zagreb. I would like to point out that these criminal proceedings against our client, Mr. Martic, was one of the numerous proceedings in absentia. The former President of the Tribunal and the Human Rights Watch pointed out that the circumstances of those proceeding were filed from equitable -- and the charges were based on the ethnic affiliations of those accused. This is a fact that our client proposed as something that was in his favour when he spoke about Croatia and the country in which he resided before he arrived at the Tribunal. Besides, this was a trial in absentia for terrorism and for insurrection against the constitutional order of a country. That would be all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. [Microphone not activated] ... with the Pre-Trial Conference. Now, there are guidelines on the standards governing the admission of evidence. Now, there is a document that I believe has been circulated. Let me just confirm. Do you have a copy it have, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. We received it just before this Pre-Trial Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Milovancevic, do you have a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We received a copy some minutes ago. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we record that the parties are agreed that that will form the guidelines for standards governing the admission of evidence, or do the parties want to read it before you make any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm confident that we will have few, if any, suggestions, but if we could have an opportunity to read it I would appreciate it, and we could make comments perhaps to the Court tomorrow, in the session tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honour. I believe this is a fair suggestion. Up until this time, we were not aware of this document. I believe these are relevant questions that will in more than one way define the proceedings before this Chamber. I think the Defence team must familiarise ourselves with everything contained in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well, then. Then we'll postpone any decision on the guidelines until tomorrow. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the question of agreed facts, it seems that both parties submitted some annexes to the pre-trial briefs concerning agreed facts but that the Prosecution on the 2nd of November, 2004, indicated that the annexes correctly reflected the agreement reached between the parties. Do you confirm that, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour the correct document reflecting the agreed facts is in fact the annex that is attached to the Defence pre-trial brief. That reflects the agreed facts in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I probably am -- was a little amiss, but I haven't seen a copy of the agreed facts as presented by the Defence. I don't know. Let me just find out from my colleagues if they do have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't look like the Chamber has copies of that document. It would be appreciated if a copy could be made available. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in reply to the OTP's pre-trial brief on the 7th of May, 2004, the Defence addressed also the agreed facts referred to in the OTP's pre-trial brief. As for these agreed facts, I believe they cannot be challenged as they were stated. Both the OTP and the Defence agree with that. This has been indicated in both the OTP pre-trial brief and our reply. Unfortunately, I do not presently have a copy of our reply, but we can certainly make an effort and have a copy delivered to the Trial Chamber unless there is another motion from the OTP or from us. But certainly we can do this for you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have just had a copy handed up to the Chamber. It is a bit illegible. We would appreciate a clearer copy, particularly because two other copies have to be made hopefully out of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's the -- Your Honour, I apologise that it's illegible. It's the only copy I have available to me, but I will certainly endeavour to get a more legible copy provided to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When do you think you can do that, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, certainly first thing tomorrow morning it could be provided, if that's agreeable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Whiting. If you could provide us with three copies tomorrow. It looks like at the Rule 65 ter Conference held on the 14th of September the parties stated that they couldn't come any nearer than the agreed facts as stated in the Defence's statements. Is it still the position? Are the parties not in any position to come any closer?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct. It's still the position that I don't believe we would be able to agree on any additional facts. It is, of course, often the case, I think, that as trial starts and the trial progresses areas of dispute are further identified and likewise areas of potential agreement are also identified. So we will always be on the lookout, as I'm sure the Defence will as well, for possibilities of further agreement once the trial starts and progresses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the position of the Defence, too, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to understand this situation about the agreed facts, it is important to keep in mind the circumstance that the OTP proposed to the Defence 45 items to agree upon. I think nearly 30 have been agreed, which is more than a few. These are important facts, and I believe this will greatly contribute to expedite these proceedings. At a Status Conference in September 2005, as Defence counsel for the accused Mr. Martic, I indicated to the Pre-Trial Judge the possibility that the Defence may offer to the OTP another set of facts to be agreed. This was in relation to augmenting the 65 ter exhibit list expanded by the Prosecution in their motion on the 19th of August 2005, now comprising 719 exhibits. On this occasion, the Pre-Trial Judge wanted the Defence to give him a figure how long we would need to analyse this new material and documents, and reach a decision on what could be agreed and what could not. We now know that this is over 6.600 pages of written documents, which pursuant to a proposal by the OTP will be tendered into evidence during the trial of Mr. Martic. Unfortunately, we are still facing a variety of problems that make it very difficult for us to review these documents. This is an extensive explanation that I've just provided, but I believe that one has been overdue. I did tell the Pre-Trial Judge that once we have studied the documents we would do our best to achieve the objectives. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. If you can just try to stick to brief answers, Mr. Milovancevic, at this stage, because we just wanted to find out what the position was in terms of the parties coming closer to one another on agreed facts. Two things that the Bench -- the Chamber would like to ask the parties about. There may be more, maybe, from my colleagues. Is it not possible for the parties to agree on a list of victims, for instance? Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's certainly -- one would think that would be an area that we could agree on, and we would be happy to agree -- that pertains specifically to certain reports concerning exhumations and there's -- we have an expert with respect to that, so that would certainly be -- we would be open to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, very briefly, is that an issue that the Defence would be disposed to negotiating?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A brief answer would be yes, under specific circumstances. The original indictment contained the names of victims but provided no personal details on those victims, their birth years and so on and so forth. We have a new list of victims now with this information entered later on. However, this is an enormous amount of documents to go through. I will endeavour to do that. I will enlist the help of an expert just like the OTP has. I believe at this point in time this will prove to be a tall order but that doesn't necessarily mean that will not be attempt to go do so once the trial itself gets going. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then the parties are urged to try and negotiate that list and try to come to an agreement on it as the trial goes on. The Chamber will keep asking about progress in that regard. The other issue that the Chamber thought of asking the parties about is whether the parties would agree that there was or there was no conflict in the relevant territories to this case. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, of course. Certainly from the point of view of the Prosecution that's something that we would welcome. I have no look again at the agreed facts. It may be in some degree already addressed in some respects on the agreed facts, but it could be something that probably could be agreed upon further. But of course the Prosecution would be happy to have that agreed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to remember offhand, Mr. Milovancevic, whether that was one of the issues agreed to by the parties, or whether it can be negotiated if it wasn't one of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order for you to understand our position, I will say this briefly: This is an indictment -- this is an indictment that encompasses the time period between 1990 and 1995. In 1991, even 1992, there is only one subject of international law. In the meantime, new subjects created. What is the nature of this conflict? Who are the warring parties? Which territories encompassed. This is a difficult and highly complex legal and factual issue. In any case, that is precisely the reason why this trial is now under way, because this was a conflict, which is a fact. However, these facts are material to the Defence and to our position. It would be premature for us to put forward a position now in the sense that you have now requested, if my understanding of what you have just said is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. One of maybe the reasons why the Chamber was asking the question, Mr. Milovancevic, is it seems at a provisional release hearing on the 26th of September, 2003, the accused stated that he admitted to the bombing of Zagreb, "for reasons which I hope will be understood why I did this." I'm not quite sure whether the Defence is able to state at this stage what the status of that statement would be and what impact it may have on the case. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour, I will try to be brief. The debate concerning provisional release of my client was conducted in 2003. The second motion for leave to grant provisional release was delivered in May 2002, but there was no reply. However, there was someone else representing the accused Mr. Martic. There was another counsel back in 2003. My client was represented by a counsel with whom he very soon after parted ways with. One thing that cannot be challenged are the posts and positions that the accused occupied at the time. He was the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. What exactly happened and how, at least that is the position of the Defence team now, is something for which certain facts will need be established but also legal issued raised relating to international law of war and conflict. That is as much as I can say for the time being, Your Honour. My colleague has just suggested the following: The Status Conference that you referred to was back in 2002. The accused surrendered in May 2002. Soon after, this Status Conference was held. I made an error. I said the first Status Conference took place in 2003 but in fact it took place in 2002. That's one correction that I wish to enter for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. I would imagine from what you have said what can be said about that statement at this stage is that the Defence is not expressing any position on that statement at this stage. Am I right, just in one word, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have understood me correctly, Your Honour. At this point in time, we think it is too early to give our final and definite position, which doesn't mean that at a later point we will not do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can we then move to the next item, item 7, the Prosecution's decision not to lead evidence regarding certain parts on Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Prosecution indicated that it would not lead evidence pertaining to crimes committed in certain parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, namely that part that I'm not able to pronounce, Prnjavor, Sipovo, and Bosanska Gradiska. However, some people who give evidence on those crimes be still scheduled to appear. It also appears that there might be some documentary evidence and the Prosecution should therefore -- I just want to find out from the Prosecution what the position is with regard to the evidence pertaining to these areas. I am aware of the notification that was filed bill the Prosecution to withdraw some of the evidence, but it looks like there are still some other witnesses or some other evidence that sort of relates to those areas. Is the Prosecution able to clear that up?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In the notice that the Court referred to, the Prosecution, as the Court said, elected -- has elected, for reasons of just expediency in trying to shorten the case and streamline it, not to pursue certain crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We tried to -- we had intended to drop all the witnesses that related to those crimes; however, I see that there are two that -- two additional witness that could be dropped and those -- on that -- on the schedule attached to that notice it's number 9, which is MM009, and Witness number MM015. All of the other witnesses, however, pertain to crime bases or crimes that are -- that continue to be pursued by the Prosecution. Those are the only two witnesses, I believe, that can be dropped. It is true that there are no doubt some documents, though probably not very many, that pertain to these crime bases that could also be dropped. We have not undertaken the exercise to go through and identify those documents on the exhibit list. I will say just to be clear that the joint criminal enterprise that is charged still includes members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, and there still will be some evidence pertaining to their participation in the joint criminal enterprise, and some -- and many of the documents and some of the witnesses will touch on that, and then of course there is one area of Bosnia and Herzegovina that remains in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I -- before you sit down, Mr. Whiting, can the Chamber accept that the Prosecution is formally withdrawing witnesses MM009 and MM015 or --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Formally withdrawing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The question of opening statements. I suppose under this point what the Chamber would like to get an idea of is how long the Prosecution anticipates the presentation of the opening statement would take.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I expect my opening to be less than the day tomorrow, and I think considerably less. I expect it to be approximately -- it will be between two and three hours is my approximation. I haven't read through it and timed it but that's my guess. But certainly considerably less than the full day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And, Mr. Milovancevic, does the Defence confirm what the Chamber has come to hear, that the Defence elects to make its opening statement, if any at all, at the opening of the Defence case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. The Defence will not use the opportunity envisaged by Rule 84, namely to present their opening statements after the opening statement of the Prosecution. We plan to do that at the beginning of our case, upon the conclusion of the Prosecution case. However, I wish to inform the Trial Chamber that the accused, Milan Martic, wishes to avail himself of his right envisaged in Rule 84 bis to use up a bit of time, about 45 minutes, after the conclusion of the Prosecution opening statement, to give his own opening statement under the guidance of the Trial Chamber. And another comment with your permission, Your Honour. In view of the information given to us by our learned friends from the Prosecution, namely Mr. Whiting, that his opening statement will take two to two and a half hours, of course it's different to know exactly how long it would last. I think that it would be possible for the accused, Mr. Martic, to give his opening statement tomorrow. I believe that there will be a sufficient time for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May not be a need for the Chamber to sit if it happens the way you suggested. Thank you very much. Can we move on then to item 9 -- outstanding motions. This is the motion -- Prosecution's motion to amend its 65 ter witness list. Is that correct? I just wanted to say that a decision will be rendered as soon as possible on -- a decision would be rendered as soon as possible on this motion if it hasn't been distributed. And then there was also the Prosecution -- did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think we received a decision on that motion. It's been distributed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And what about the decision on the Prosecution's motion for admission of witness statements pursuant to Rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There we have not received a decision Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It will be handed down fairly soon, okay? The Chamber is aware of the fact that the Prosecution has not produced full statements of some of the Prosecution witnesses. Is that correct, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a matter on which various Trial Chambers have different views and so we'll be guided by this Trial Chamber and its preferences. Some Trial Chambers don't want the full statements of Prosecution witnesses; others do. If it's this Chamber's desire to have the prior statements of the witnesses who will testify, that's something that we can undertake to provide to the Chamber in some kind of a systematic way. With the understanding that with some witnesses that will be voluminous material. There are witnesses who have -- who not only have an ICTY statement but who have testified in previous trials or who have multiple statements. So in some cases that could be voluminous, but that's no problem to provide to the Court in some form, perhaps electronic, perhaps hard copy, whatever the preference is. I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Your Honour. My colleague has just indicated that perhaps the Court is asking about -- is referring to delayed disclosure of some witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well, there are certain witnesses for whom delayed disclosure as a protective measure was granted, and I believe in every case it was -- what was ordered was that the Prosecution disclose the prior statements of the witnesses to the Defence 30 days before the witness testifies and that's something that we're mindful of and we'll do. As the case progresses we will disclose that's statements to the Defence. Now, that, again, is a separate matter from whether the Trial Chamber wants to have the statements disclosed to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It wasn't my understanding that we wanted the statements disclosed to the Trial Chamber, it was just for them to be discovered to the opposite party.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. That's something we're mindful of and as the schedule -- as we determine the schedule of witnesses, we're aware of the 30-day requirement. In cases -- in one case I think ten days has been ordered, and we will keep up with that schedule and make sure we comply with those orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I believe there is also a practice of [Microphone not activated] - I'm sorry - proofing notes which are usually given a day before a witness testifies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- that's something that's been followed in some cases and not in others, and it was not our -- it was not our intention -- in the last trial I just finished, it's not something that we did nor was required. It was not my intention to do it in this case. What we do do, of course, is when we meet with witnesses before they testify and prepare their testimony, if there are matters that arise in those discussions, for example, new -- new information or any changes, substantial changes in information, that of course is disclosed immediately to the Defence by way of a memo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the Chamber makes a ruling, let's just find out what the attitude of the Defence is on the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when it comes to witnesses with protection measures, it is true that the Prosecution has an obligation to deliver to the Defence 30 days before the trial commences information about their identity. We're now facing two issues here, from what day the 30-day period starts running and another issue which is much more important and which would significantly improve the efficiency of our work and make the life of the Defence much easier, and this is the list of the witnesses that the Prosecution could disclose to the Defence so that the Defence could plan its time, organise its work, study all the issues in a timely manner. Thus we expect the Trial Chamber to be along -- to pass a decision along those lines, to issue an order that would cover all of these issues. It would also be very useful for the Defence to know 30 days in advance the chronology of the proposed testimony. And the same will apply for us once we begin with our case. It would be good for the Defence to have an idea at least what is planned. We understand that not everything can be envisaged in advance, that not all of the details can be planned ahead, but whatever is possible to be disclosed should be disclosed to us now to facilitate our work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. Your Honour, if I could address some of the points raised by Defence counsel. With respect to the starting point for the 30-day disclosure, the order of the Court is it's 30 days before the witness testifies, and that's what -- the practice that we will be following. With respect to witness order, we will do our best to provide the witness order that -- as we know it in a timely fashion. 30 days is not -- is not very realistic. It's just impossible with various witness schedules and issues in terms of scheduling that come into play, it's impossible to know 30 days in advantage. We'll know certainly I believe before Christmas we'll know who our first several witnesses will be in January, and then we will keep the Defence updated as we schedule witnesses, and that will always be one or two weeks ahead of time. This case is not so big that we -- it's only going to last for a few months. It only has 40 or 50 witnesses. It's not so big that I think it's necessary to have -- to try to impose 30 days ahead of time. I don't think that's ever been done in a trial. Finally, with respect to the proofing summary, the Prosecution of course has provided summaries, 65 ter summaries of all of its witnesses. It expects the witnesses to testify largely according to those summaries and is happy to indicate to the Court if there's going to be any deviation from those summaries. Frankly, preparing a proofing sum Rule while you're trying to prepare the witnesses who are here for a limited amount of time and to keep the trial going can be quite an onerous burden on top of having to provide the -- on top of having already provided the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just say thank you very much, Mr. Whiting, for first of all responding to the issues raised by Mr. Milovancevic but also for the last point you make, which is actually what was under discussion. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission I would like to raise an issue which seems to be quite important to me. It has to do with the status of some of the motions of the Prosecution. It is expected that they will be ruled upon soon. However, at the 65 ter Conference held on the 22nd of November, we learned that there is a large number of the Prosecution motions relating to 94 bis, which has to do with the experts, and Rule 92 bis. At the meeting, I raised an issue which is quite an important. It is first and foremost a problem for the Defence, but I think it's also relevant to the Trial Chamber. We do not know what status 28 witnesses have. These are the witnesses that in accordance with the OTP motion will be involved under Rule 94 bis. This was raised in the OTP motion submitted in February of 2005. We responded to all of these motions. However, it is quite difficult for us to envisage how much work this will entail, because at this point in time we still do not know what these witnesses will be testifying about and whether we will be at all given an opportunity to cross-examine these witnesses. These are the issues that are outstanding, that need yet to be resolved and that will greatly reflect both the work of the Defence and the Prosecution. Another issue now that we're dealing with witnesses is this: Your Honours, we heard what the Prosecution said today about three locations in Bosnia. I'm not quite sure that I made accurate notation when it comes to Prnjavor, Sipovo, and Bosanska Gradiska. We do not understand whether the Prosecution will drop charges regarding these locations or the Prosecution namely is withdrawing the witnesses who are to testify about these locations. Another problem is that in their pre-trial brief, the Prosecution says that certain cases mentioned in the indictment are just examples or samples of the acts attributed to the accused through joint criminal enterprise. So this is a very delicate issue for the Defence. Based on what my learned friend Mr. Whiting said today, we took it that the Prosecution will simply withdraw these witnesses but that the facts named in the indictment and the pre-trial brief remain in force. Therefore, I would like to be given a clarification, and I apologise in advance if I misunderstood some of what was said today. I would need to know the answer to this query. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, thank you so much for raising that issue. You just ran one little step ahead of the Chamber. We were going to get to the 92 bis and 94 bis issues. I suppose as regards the Prosecution's decision about the charges relating to those areas that they say they are not going to lead evidence on, Mr. Whiting can perhaps tell us whether he's dropping the charges or just withdrawing the witnesses. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we are doing is just withdrawing the witnesses. We're just not going to lead evidence on those specific charges. Dropping the charges would require amending the indictment which is a slightly complicated process and I don't think would -- it would take a lot of time and wouldn't advance anything. So it -- the same effect is achieved by simply not pursuing those -- the evidence on those charges. But again to be clear because it was raised I think by Mr. Milovancevic, we do still allege the joint criminal enterprise as it is charged in the indictment and as it is described in the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- you are withdrawing the charges in substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, in substance the effect is that, Your Honour, but those charges, of course, are mixed together with charges that are remaining. So, for example, there is no count of the indictment that is being dropped. There are just parts of counts. So, for example, there are murders. There is a series of murders that are alleged in the indictment and they are all charged as a count of extermination and murder. Some of those murders. The ones that occurred in Bosnia and Herzegovina in those particular areas that are identified will not be pursued, but the other murders are still going to be pursued. So the count remains in the indictment. So all the counts remain. All the counts will be proven, it's just parts of counts and evidence related to certain counts that will not be pursued. I hope I have been clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You were very clear, but it seems to me also that you would have to go through each very carefully, and maybe at the end of the day consider what courses you are going to drop in all fairness to the accused in respect to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I appreciate Your Honour, and I am certainly mindful to be fair to the accused and to alert the accused what we're doing here and what we're not pursuing, and I hope we have been clear in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission. The accused must understand the charges against him. We are currently trying to establish the number of witnesses. It used to be 79, and perhaps once these witness are withdrawn the number of witnesses will be reduced. However, Mr. Whiting just told us that the substance of the indictment remains the same. The counts remain as they were, which means that maybe the number of witnesses will remain the same, but they will be testifying about different events. However, whatever the case, the indictment must be clear to us. We must know what we have to defend ourselves against. We have to know what our client is charged with. Therefore, the Prosecution needs to bring their pre-trial brief in conformity with the new indictment, because we cannot be expected to get what is it that the Prosecution is trying to say. It would be a very dangerous situation for the Defence. And in that regard, I fully agree with the view of the Trial Chamber, but I think it needs to be reiterated. I think that we must have a completely clear situation whether it comes to the rights of the accused. He must know exactly what he's charged with. Another matter. My learned friend Mr. Whiting said that these three locations are related to the so-called joint criminal enterprise, and the nature of this enterprise is described in such a way that the leadership of Bosnian Serbs and some other people who are tried here before this Tribunal have been accused for the same acts as the accused Martic. Therefore, there is the responsibility that these locations that are dropped in this case will be complemented by some other witnesses who will be testifying about other events. I am raising this so that we can all get some idea about the amount of work where -- that we will be faced with here. Perhaps everything is clear to the Prosecution, but the Defence and Trial Chamber must also fully understand the intentions of the Prosecution. Perhaps I took a bit too long, Your Honours, but I was just trying to explain the situation as we see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting, do you want to take a second bite of the cherry to try and explain yourself, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, you read my mind. That's exactly what I'd like to do. Your Honour, as the Court is aware but I'm not sure if Defence counsel has this at hand, the Prosecution filed on the 23rd of November a revised list of witnesses, and I hope that is something that's available -- been made available, served on the Defence. That list has 65 witnesses, not 79. And as indicated by the Prosecution at the beginning of the session this evening, we've dropped two more. So we're down to 63 witnesses. What we have indicated in that filing is that we will not pursue any matters related to Prnjavor, Sipovo, and Bosanska Gradiska. What that means very simply, and it's not complicated, is that where there are references to those three places in the indictment, evidence will not be led. So for example, in paragraphs 35 and 36, there are murders alleged in those places. We will not lead evidence on those paragraphs. So it's -- it is a very simple matter, and I agree that the Defence has to be on notice about what the case is going to be, but it is frankly a very simple matter to now look again at the indictment and at the pre-trial brief to see what is no longer going to be pursued by the Prosecution. It is simply the matters related to those three areas, end of story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that is now clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Is it something new or is it by extension? Is it something new or is it by extension?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just about this last sentence of my learned colleague, if I may. I have a great concern that what the OTP has just suggested is legally impossible. There can be no indictment in relation to three different places and killings without evidence. The OTP has just informed us that they abide by the allegations of the original indictment and the relevant paragraphs but that there will be no evidence to support those allegations. Now, how are we to understand that, Your Honour? Either those locations and the relevant paragraphs are part of the indictment and are dealt with, or, if the OTP has no supporting material, let them give the whole thing up. I must say I'm trying to understand the legal logic behind this, that is at work here. It seems that facts are irrelevant whether something is proven or not. I'm merely talking about what the OTP has just informed us about. Whenever there is evidence to Prnjavor, Sipovo, and Bosanska Gradiska and the killings at those locations, we will not be bringing any evidence but however the indictment stays as it is. What is the Defence supposed to do with such an indictment and with these paragraphs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I'm not quite sure what the problem to the Defence is. Obviously the Prosecution has drafted its indictment in the manner in which it has done, and it has alleged crimes taking place at various places. If its in wisdom the Prosecution decides not to call evidence that relates to certain areas, that goes to the question of proof of those allegations irrespective of whether or not they were on the indictment. I don't think that it is something that we should be taking too much time on. If they have not proved the commission of those crimes in these specific areas it's up to the Defence to argue so at the end of the trial. I don't think we can dictate to the Prosecution to withdraw those charges simply because it decides not to lead evidence on those instances. Okay. I think that will close that point. In the interests of trying to limit the duration of the trial, I'm going to try and press a little harder on you, Mr. Whiting. To the extent that any of the witnesses that the Prosecution intends to call corroborating other witnesses, is it not possible to that extent to bring in 92 bis evidence of those corroborating witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have tried to do that as much as possible, and we have asked, of course, the Court to accept under Rule 92 bis a considerable number of witness statements, and as -- with respect to certain -- with respect to each crime base, as it's referred to, we have -- we typically have one -- no, not one two, two or three witnesses coming to testify live and then all the other witnesses testifying 92 -- or submitting their evidence 92 bis as corroboration. It's, I think, not possible to limit -- to get down to one witness per crime base because these crime bases are not just one single event. They are events that occur over -- as the Court will see in the indictment, they're events that occur over a period of months, and each witness has -- for example, there will be in Saborsko or Skabrnja, it is alleged that there will be shelling that occurs, and then various attacks on the village, and then the actual final assault on the village. Well, the witnesses that we've called live will give different parts of the story. It's very rare -- very unusual that one witness is capable of telling the entire story about what happened. Some witnesses are there for the beginning, some are there only for the middle of it. So we have tried to pare down the list and be as efficient as possible. But we will -- that's something that we'll continue to look at and as the trial progresses we will be very ready -- if we feel we have proved a seven part of the case or provided sufficient evidence to the case we will be very prepared to drop witnesses as the case goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the Chamber is mindful of the facts that incidents happen all over and you're not going to call one witness and just say others must corroborate. Obviously if there's need to testify about other areas of the same area, and the first witness has not seen that part, there is a need to call a second or a third or subsequent witness to cover these areas. It's entirely with respect to corroborating witnesses that the question was raised. The next question relates to expert witnesses and the witnesses with special expertise relating to exhibits, exhumations, and intercepted conversations. I'm not quite sure whether the Chamber is correct in saying there had not been any responses from the Defence with respect to those two sets of witnesses. And if the Chamber is correct that there has not been any response from the Defence, the question would be, can't that evidence be tendered in terms of Rule 94 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could just have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my understanding that there was a response from the Defence with respect to the experts that we submit it via rule 94 bis, and it's my understanding that all of the experts at this time are challenged by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that include even the experts relating to exhumations, exhibits, and other things?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It refers to -- yes, the experts relating to exhumations, towards -- to our military expert, and to our expert relating to the effects of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just to recap, is it therefore the position of the Prosecution that at this stage 63 witnesses will be called for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. If we may move on to the scheduling of the trial now. If -- yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honour, just briefly. I would like to repeat this fact. On the 25th of February, 2005, the OTP filed an expert opinion, military expert opinion, in relation to Rule 94 bis, something that we challenged at the time. It was in the same motion that the OTP moved to have the transcripts admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis. There are two motions that we made in relation to this motion on the 25th of February when the Defence received Mladen Loncar's statement or opinion pursuant to 94 bis, followed by a motion that pursuant to 92 bis his transcript from a previous trial should be admitted. There has not been any ruling so far on these two motions. On the 25th of -- on the 28th of February, 2005 there was another expert opinion which we have replied to. Only the 29th of February, 2004, there has been Davor Strinovic's expert opinion, plus a motion by the OTP to have his transcripts admitted. We have replied to both of these motions, and we are still awaiting a decision. On the 28th of February 2005, we received expert Ivan Grujic's opinion pursuant to Rule 94 bis or, rather, the OTP forwarded this motion to both the Chamber and the Defence and another motion that pursuant to 92 bis, Rule 92 bis, the transcripts of this expert should be admitted. We have replied to both these motions. Finally on the 28th of February, 2005, a written filing, a motion by the OTP to introduce written statements and live witnesses pursuant to Rule 92 bis. Our reply was sent on the 21st of April, 2005, and the Prosecution replied on the 28th of April, 2005. I would also like to remind you that there is the OTP motion of the 19th of July, 2005 -- or, rather, excuse me, the 17th of August, 2005. The previous one was ruled upon. One is a motion to expand the list of witnesses. There was a ruling. And the next is the 17th of August, 2005, not ruled upon for the 65 ter exhibit list to be expanded by 719 exhibits. Not ruled upon yet. This is a great number of new exhibits. I'm mentioning this now because at the outset today the Defence drew the Chamber's attention to one difficulty we are facing. If I can have the Chamber's understanding on this, please. We have a problem understanding the way in which the testimony of these experts will be treated and which witness statements will be viewed and treated. We have 28 witnesses where we don't know what sort of evidence they will give, whether it will be a partial 92 bis or whether they will have a different status. We believe that a ruling on these matters would determine the length of this trial, and to a large extent our work as well as the OTP's work. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Just for the guidance of the Chamber, can you very briefly tell us how many motions are outstanding and what they are, without expanding on them, just so we know exactly what should be attended to for -- before the trial continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're talking about seven OTP motions in relation to Rule 94 bis and 92(B) or a different paragraph, including the motion for leave to expand the witness list. The Defence has, of course, replied to each and every one of these. These, needless to say, are motions that -- I need to remind the Chamber of one thing here. These were filed as early as February this year to the previous Trial Chamber. These have not been dealt with. And just another detail. The President of the Tribunal ruled on the Prosecution's proposal for joinder. This case was forwarded to a third Chamber, and this Chamber was supposed to rule on this proposal. On the 4th of July, 2001, this was returned to the original Chamber because of all the outstanding motions that had not been dealt with, so that the joinder would not halt the proceedings and the rulings that were to be made. This has not been dealt with but that just means we have another fact that we need to face. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm still not quite clear how many motions there are still outstanding. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll try to address that though I don't have the dates of the motions at my fingertips. But we can provide them if that's helpful. There is a motion with respect to expand the 65 ter exhibit list. The Chamber has ruled on the witness list, expanding the witness list but there is a separate motion with respect to the exhibit list. Secondly, there is the 92 bis motion which has been discussed. That is still outstanding. Third, there is 94 bis motions with respect to the experts. And fourth, there is a protective measures motion with respect to witnesses that has also been filed and not ruled on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will attend to those outstanding motions as soon as possible. I guess we can now move on to the scheduling of the trial. According to the dates that the Chamber is in possession of, it looks like after the 14th of December, the next trial date for this case would be the 9th of January. And I think the Chamber has also received a submission from the Prosecution, or some request from the Prosecution, that the matter not proceed on the 9th and 11th of January. Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll note that on the 11th of January we're not even scheduled for a full session. I think it's an hour and a half of time on the 11th of January. So for various reasons which I can address if the Chamber would like me to, I think we would ask that we not sit the 9th and the 11th but we start the following week when we have the full week, start on the 16th. Those reasons have to do with scheduling witnesses with the holiday that the Serb Orthodox holiday and also with disclosure matters because that's already less than 30 days from today. So there's a problem with disclosure in terms of satisfying the order with delayed disclosure. So we would -- and then finally it's -- it would be very difficult to fit a witness into that time, especially with the first witness that's going -- I'm concerned that we will have a witness signature here for a week if we're not able to finish the witness in that short time that's been provided to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By holiday are you talking about holiday on the 10th?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. My understanding is that the Serb Orthodox Christmas is on January 7th, and Defence counsel may know better than me about this but that's my understanding. That's an important holiday which makes it difficult to bring a witness before the 9th in order to be able to testify on the Monday. I foresee -- this is always a scheduling difficulty for witnesses and I foresee it being a problem here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you have any comment to make on the Prosecution's request that the Court -- the Chamber doesn't sit on the 9th and the 11th? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objections to that request. We agree, Your Honour. I do have a different issue that I wish to raise, though, if I may, in connection with the very beginning of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for the time allowed me. I'll be to be very brief. On the 22nd of November, a Status Conference, a 65 ter Conference was scheduled, a meeting that was graced by your presence, Your Honour. On this occasion, the Defence team pointed out a number of difficulties that we were facing. I will not be going into those now. We received a decision of the Trial Chamber in relation to our motion dated the 18th of March, 2005. Therefore, on the 18th of March, 2005, which is nearly nine months ago, we filed an urgent motion with the previous Trial Chamber in relation to our status. I will now be speaking about what occurred on the 22nd of November. On that day, the senior legal officer for the previous Chamber, the case has in the meantime been handed over to you following an extensive discuss, he said did he not understand the problems faced by the Defence. Mr. Harhoff said that Mr. Martic was being charged with a very short period of time and a mere handful of locations as crime base, and did he not understand what sort of difficulty the Defence team were facing, he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you Mr. Milovancevic, because for the simple reason that item you are talking about we will talk about. It's provided for on the agenda, and can we just dispose of the scheduling of the trial as it stands there and we'll come back to the point you are raising, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you have indicated that you have no objection to the Court not sitting on the 9th and the 11th. I suppose I'm right there. The next date, then, is a whole week starting from the 16th of January up to the 20th. Is that okay? Can we sit on that day? Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Excuse me if I'm using strong words, but we were shocked to learn or I was shocked to learn that the senior legal officer did not understand the complex nature of the task of the Defence team on this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I again ask you, Mr. Milovancevic, we will talk about that problem. Can we for now try to focus on that little calendar that stands on your agenda if you do have it before you. If you don't have it I can rattle the dates and so -- we will talk about the problems that you are experiencing, but can we just deal with the scheduling of the case at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. I really did not understand you. You talked about the 16th of January through the 20th of January. That is beyond dispute as far as the Defence team is concerned. We looked at the scheduling, and I have nothing else to add on that particular issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I then take it that that scheduling that goes up to the 3rd of March is agreed on? In other words, after the 20th of January there's going to be 26th and the 7th, 30th and 31st of January, and it's going to be 6, 7, 16, 17, 20, 21 of February, and 2nd and 3rd of March. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine with the Prosecution, Your Honour. Obviously this usual schedule of two days here, four days, this could present difficulties at time with witnesses and scheduling but we'll deal with those as we come and we will -- we will do our best to fill all the time that has been scheduled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Does the Defence also confirm that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm afraid I might be misunderstood. I bear in mind what you have just told us, but we have something else on the agenda, and if I may be allowed to question this. With no intention to enter into a polemic with the Trial Chamber, I do not have this possibility nor would I myself be prone to do anything like that. But there is another difficult that the Defence team is face so to say anything else on this matter would make no sense and that's why I tried to say something about it a while ago but I failed to fully understand what Your Honour was saying. As for the beginning of the trial, the scheduling and the timetable is something that must be complied with once this has been ruled upon by the Trial Chamber. There's an essential issue that the Defence wishes to raise before such time, and we believe that this might affect the Chamber's position on when to begin and how to begin. If I may say something about that, I think this would greatly affect the scheduling and your ideas of the scheduling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Can you proceed, then, state the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'll be very brief. We received your decision on our motion of the 18th of March saying, among other things, that during this break from the 13th and the 14th of December until the trial continues in January, the Defence will have an opportunity to catch up with the Trial Chamber. This is a real problem for our Defence team, and that is why we request the Chamber's attention in order to deal with this issue. Were the Defence team to accept this, that would mean that we're bringing upon ourselves the obligation to have little time, only as much as a fortnight with Christmas included, to master this material that the OTP have been working on for the past 19 months throughout which time the Defence have had no investigators of our own or any means to conduct any research. This is simply put an impossible task for the Defence. We cannot catch up because the time is too short. A while ago I drew the Chamber attention to a position expressed by a previous Chamber. I'm talking about the essence of the difficulty the Defence is facing. It's an assessment of the previous Trial Chamber. No reasonable person could say you should assume their responsibility but the case has been handed over to you and you are the Trial Chamber that must create fair conditions for an equitable trial. At this point in time, since March 2004, the Defence has had no opportunity to hire investigators. We were denied this opportunity. We got the pre-trial brief. We got the extension of the witness list. 60 -- 24.000 pages of documents and 68 CDs, in short. We are expected to catch up with all this and only given very little time to work with. My understanding is the first Chamber that dealt with the case did not review the magnitude of the entire case. My colleague, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, on the 20th of May, 2004, stated at a Status Conference that the Martic case would elicit a large number of complex legal issues, very many issues to do with the joint criminal enterprise would be correlating with many other cases, the Milosevic case, the Plavsic case, the Babic case, the Mladic case, the Seselj case, the Stanisic case, the Simatovic case, and a number of other cases would be involved, and all of this is under paragraph 6 of the indictment. Their names are listed there. We have the amended indictment. We started this conference today by a reference to this amended indictment. After the original indictment was raised in 1995, the accused Martic is being charged with new charges altogether. Nineteen counts in relation to five years of which he was the incumbent of the following posts: Defence Minister, president of the republic, and so on and so forth. He was active in two different countries. This was between 1990 and 1995. One of the previously sovereign states disintegrated - that was Yugoslavia - and new countries were created. A conflict occurred, the nature of which we are bound to determine. Our requests are refused. Our requests to be able to get on with work are refused. The pre-trial stage takes 43 months, whereas the pre-trial stage should normally take between 6 and eight months. This one has been going on for 43 months. So over the last couple of months the Defence has not been able to keep up with the OTP. We would like to indicate to you the dramatic nature of our position. We must think out loud about this. Mr. Harhoff told us that this was a simple case with only several locations involved over a brief period of time, whereas in actual fact we are talking about the duration of the entire conflict, five years, the entire duration of the joint criminal enterprise of which Mr. Martic is a key leader. We believe that the problem faced by the Defence lay in the lack of understanding by the previous Trial Chamber. This is also indicated by the number of outstanding motions. If those had been dealt with probably we would be facing a very different picture now. Forgive me for saying this, but the Defence are facing a very dramatic position now. Contrary to Article 21 of the Statute, contrary to Article 7(3)(B) of the human rights convention, contrary to judgements that have been passed, Mawzit vs. Russia, January 2005, contrary to a judgement of this Tribunal in the Krajisnik case specifying that no restrictions can be imposed on Defence teams, that Defence teams must be allowed to prepare their cases for trial, we now have a situation where we're facing a period of 15 weeks. We have gone on without means, without funds for so long to catch up. We're trying to keep up with the OTP but the first indictment was filed in 1995, and the last motion to expand the exhibit list was the 18th of August, 2005 containing 6.600 pages of potentially exculpatory material but this material must be reviewed all these documents must be reviewed analysed. I will just say one more thing, Your Honour. We as a Defence team must now embark upon this trial not having been allowed to enlist the help of experts to track down our own witnesses, to collect evidence, to devise a consistent Defence plan. On the 16th of January the trial will begin, and if everything happens the way it now looks we shall just not be able to cross-examine witnesses. The OTP have spent ten years preparing the case. Are we supposed to do the same thing over the next 15 days? We have given it our best shop Your Honours but this is a physical impossibilities. We are trying to keep this case afloat. We have been trying to keep up. We have been filing all the replies. Maybe I'm being a bit too extensive for which I apologise to the Trial Chamber. I just wish to show that facing a difficult situation, an uphill struggle, being asked to do the impossible, we have done our best. We replied to motions by the OTP just to keep damage from being inflicted to our client in a situation where we were hardly able to do anything else. Therefore, we are dealing here with the best interest of justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And all we want to have is a fair trial, equality of arms. We would like a more reasonable deadline to master these documents. We would like that to be granted to us by the Trial Chamber. I have pointed this out on many occasions, but we met with a lack of understanding. We were wondering what's going on? And it is now that we realise that the previous Trial Chamber have left so many motions unresolved, and what they lack is a clear picture of the complex nature of the case before us. The joint criminal enterprise comprises the entire indictment. It is directly addressed by paragraphs 2 through 9 and in the pre-trial brief from 37 to through 54 of the pre-trial brief. Factual description and the substance of the joint criminal enterprise that the OTP are referencing. So much for me Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will take a break. We'll come back at 8.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to say, Mr. Milovancevic, the points you made just before we went for the break were the points I kept on saying we will deal with in the next item. I want to believe that we have exhausted what you have to say on that item. I just want to say the following: First of all, this Chamber gave a decision on there point denying your motion for a postponement. I don't think it is appropriate that the issues that were dealt with in that decision should be raised again in this hearing today. Secondly, in your submissions this afternoon on this point, you made a reference to the fact that the decision denying the postponement had indicated that the Defence would get an opportunity to do their preparations because the trial would not be scheduled that early. Now, that decision led on the relevant point that "Considering that the presentation of evidence through witnesses will not start until at the earliest the second week of January 2006 at a date to be determined at the Pre-Trial Conference which would allow the accused adequate time to prepare his defence." Now, the scheduling as discussed today, if this case had started on the 9th of January, would have been at least at the beginning of the week. The schedule is now scheduled for 16th of January, which is at the beginning of the third week. So I do not think that the scheduling is inconsistent with the decision given, and the Chamber is of the view, therefore, that the point you've made on that that you were not being given the opportunity you were promised in the decision not correct. There is no the papers that were filed with the Chamber a letter, if I can find it, which I seem to remember that it's dated the 8th of December, 2005, in which OLAD advises the Defence about the developments in the very issue that you raised. And in that letter, the Defence is being asked to file its submissions on the complexity of the matter in the trial stage, which means that OLAD is prepared to review the -- or at least to consider those submissions from the Defence as relates to the trial stage of the case. And if the Defence has not made those submissions yet, the Defence is invited to make those submissions. If the Defence has made those submissions and OLAD has not replied, I think the Defence must await the reply of OLAD. Fourthly, the Chamber is of the view that given the scheduling as it stands, with a number of openings in between the dates of hearing, the Defence should be in a position to prepare its case as the trial proceeds. And finally, just like I would imagine the Defence would think, the Chamber is of the view that justice delayed is justice denied. Now, the accused has been in detention for a very long period. The Chamber is concerned to bring this matter to finality as speedily as possible, and it doesn't appear as if postponements that can be avoided should be granted easily. The Chamber is therefore of the view that item 10, which was the last item on the agenda -- beg your pardon, item 12, should be adequately dealt with between the Defence and OLAD in terms of that correspondence of the 8th of December, 2005. Is there any comment, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood, Your Honour. I just wish to mention one issue. Initially you asked Mr. Martic about his health. As I visited him today at the Detention Unit, we informed the Chamber on the 22nd of November, the Chamber and the Registry, that Mr. Martic has a problem with his right shoulder and right arm. The pain is so bad that it wakes him up at night. So far the doctors have not responded to his complaints. Therefore, I would like to ask the Trial Chamber, if it is authorised to do so, to instruct the Registry that the accused be given medical assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised, Mr. Milovancevic, that this is a matter which requires the Defence to -- let me backtrack. This is a matter to be addressed to the head of the Detention Unit, and the head of the Detention Unit would then take it upon him. I'm not quite sure how it has been dealt with so far. It may very well be it has been dealt with orally, and if that be the case, may I suggest that maybe you might be prepared to help Mr. Martic to make a written presentation to the head of the unit tabulating his problems and asking assistance from him. In the meantime the Chamber will also be investigating what other options may be available to Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one sentence, Your Honour, with your permission, in order to clarify. The Defence would apply to the Detention Unit had -- had it not been for the fact that during our previous Pre-Trial Conference Mr. Harhoff instructed us to apply to the Registry. So we were awaiting further instructions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Counsel, have you already addressed a request to the Registry and not succeeded or not received a response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I raised this issue at the 65 ter meeting held on the 22nd of November. It was not attended by the accused Mr. Martic. I raised this issue saying that he had had for four months shoulder pains, that his arm is -- has atrophied, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, sorry, just a second. I think the question from the Judge was, since the 65 ter Conference have you applied to the Registry and have you been successful or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I have not understood you. Not since then, no. I have only just arrived to The Hague today, and I only had contact with my client today. This is why I raised this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... interim?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, Your Honours, Mr. Martic is the kind of a person who dislikes complaining. He simply suffers quietly. However, once I go and visit him in the Detention Unit, when I see how he makes his movements when pouring coffee or something else, when I see how painful these movements are, it is only then that I'm able to recognise the extent of the pain. Otherwise, he's the kind of a person that doesn't complain. And upon seeing this, I felt this need to raise this issue. This is not something that he would normally mention when talking to me on the phone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So you will now formally address your request to the Registry?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept your suggestion, Your Honours. That's precisely what we're going to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that brings us to the end of our Pre-Trial Conference. The matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I just want to make clear what I think is probably already clear, but -- that we will start with witnesses on the 16th of January, then? Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is the position. Thanks, Mr. Whiting. And, Mr. Whiting, we also hope that the Prosecution will, as soon as possible, give us the order of the witnesses, and also to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Unless anybody has anything to say, I think that brings us to the end of the Pre-Trial Conference. The Court will stand adjourned until the 16th -- I beg your pardon, until tomorrow.
